introduction: Bahá’u’lláh defines justice in an unexpected place: it is, first, to see with one’s own eyes and not through the eyes of others, to be free of idle fancy and imitation. From that inward beginning the readings widen. Justice is giving each his due, and having no regard for one’s own advantage; it is the light of statesmanship, upheld by reward and punishment; it asks for fair wages and a share for workers, laws that protect society from the wrongdoer, and rulers who answer to a divine balance. The later readings say that this justice has appeared and that most people have not noticed, promise the oppressor his recompense, and end in prayer. The prophets of Israel, the Qur’an, Plato, Aristotle, Augustine and Confucius are placed beside the readings. So are those who doubted that justice is anything but power, Thrasymachus, the Athenians at Melos and Hobbes, with Lear on how wealth hides guilt, Pascal on a justice that changes at a river, and Jesus’ command to turn the other cheek.
questions: Bahá’u’lláh calls it the essence of justice to look into all things with a searching eye and to be free of imitation. Why should fairness to others begin with how one sees?
Thrasymachus said that justice is the interest of the stronger, and the Athenians that the strong do what they can. What in these readings, and in your own experience, answers them?
The readings give an injured person no right to pardon a crime that harms society; Jesus said to turn the other cheek. What belongs to the individual, and what to the community?
One reading asks that workers be given a share of profits. Is that justice or generosity, and what difference does the answer make?
Lear says that robes and furred gowns hide all. Where today is justice still not carried out in all classes?
Several readings say that the sun of justice has risen and that people do not perceive it. What would you expect to see in a society that had begun to perceive it?

outside.why: Leviticus forbids both partialities: thou shalt not respect the person of the poor, nor honour the person of the mighty.

Lear, mad on the heath, says that through tattered clothes small vices appear, while robes and furred gowns hide all. How far has justice in any age been carried out in all classes, from the highest to the lowest?
Plato's Socrates arrives at a definition of the same family: justice is doing one's own business, and not being a busybody.
Aristotle reports the saying that justice is the greatest of virtues, and that neither evening nor morning star is so wonderful.
Kant made the same demand of his century: have the courage to use your own understanding.
The Qur’an asks believers to be staunch in justice, witnesses for God even though it be against themselves or their kindred, whether the case be of a rich man or a poor.

Thrasymachus, in Plato's Republic, proclaims that justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger. What evidence is there that anyone acts with no regard for personal benefit, and what does justice require where that evidence is thin?
Leviticus commands just balances, just weights and a just measure in every dealing with a neighbour.
Paul asked the Corinthians why they did not rather take wrong and suffer themselves to be defrauded than go to law with one another. When is it right to refuse to be cheated, and when to bear it?
Justice Harlan wrote in dissent in 1896 that the constitution is colour-blind, and that in respect of civil rights all citizens are equal before the law.
Augustine asked: justice being taken away, what are kingdoms but great robberies?
Amos asks that judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream.
The psalm joins the same pairs: mercy and truth are met together; righteousness and peace have kissed each other.
Portia says that mercy seasons justice, and that in the course of justice none of us should see salvation. Where does a kingdom founded on both draw the line between them?
Moses charges the judges: ye shall not respect persons in judgment; ye shall hear the small as well as the great.
Jethro advised Moses to choose able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness.
Isaiah puts it as a programme: seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow.
Confucius thought that people led by laws and punishments learn only to avoid them, while those led by virtue learn shame. Are reward and punishment the pillars of order, or its scaffolding?
Pascal wrote that justice without might is helpless, and might without justice is tyrannical.
Isaiah says that the work of righteousness shall be peace, and its effect quietness and assurance for ever.
The writing on the king's wall said: thou art weighed in the balances, and art found wanting.
A disciple of Confucius examined himself each day on three points before he judged anyone else.
Jesus says that with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again.
Plato held that cities will have no rest from evils until philosophers are kings. Is fitness for a position a matter of merit alone, and who is fit to judge it?
Proverbs says that a false balance is abomination to the Lord, but a just weight is His delight.
Mill observed that he who knows only his own side of the case knows little of that.
The psalm says: some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we will remember the name of the Lord.

The Athenians told the Melians that right is in question only between equals in power: the strong do what they can and the weak suffer what they must. On what grounds can it be said that the hosts of justice are the mightiest?
Micah's summary begins with it: what doth the Lord require of thee, but to do justly?
David's last words say that he who rules over men must be just, and shall be as the light of the morning.
Proverbs says that the throne of the king who faithfully judges the poor shall be established for ever.
Job describes his own days as a magistrate: I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame, and the cause I knew not I searched out.
Isaiah says of the just ruler that with righteousness he shall judge the poor and reprove with equity for the meek.
The psalm prays that the king be given God's judgments, and says the mountains shall then bring peace to the people.
Jeremiah reminded a king of his father: he judged the cause of the poor and needy; then it was well with him.
The psalm warns: put not your trust in princes. How should a religious community speak of rulers who treat it fairly, without flattering them?
Proverbs says that when the righteous are in authority the people rejoice.
The first letter to Timothy asks for prayers for kings and all in authority.
Machiavelli advised princes that it is safer to be feared than loved. What does this prayer assume about the source of a government's lasting strength?
Hannah sings that the Lord brings low and lifts up, and raises the poor out of the dust.
Bentham argued that the law should protect animals because the question is not whether they can reason but whether they can suffer.
Isaiah says that the Lord shall judge among the nations, and they shall beat their swords into ploughshares.
Martin Luther King wrote from a jail that injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.
Proverbs says that righteousness exalts a nation, but sin is a reproach to any people.
Adam Smith held that commerce runs on each party's regard for his own interest. What does commerce need from justice that self-interest does not supply?
Deuteronomy commands that a poor hired servant be paid on his day, before the sun goes down, for he sets his heart upon it.
James says that the hire of the labourers, kept back by fraud, cries out.
Oscar Wilde thought the proper aim was to reconstruct society on such a basis that poverty would be impossible, and distrusted charity as a remedy. Is a share in profits justice or generosity?
Mill doubted in 1848 whether all the mechanical inventions yet made had lightened the day's toil of any human being.
Jesus gave fairness its shortest rule: whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them.
Hobbes held that where there is no common power there is no law, and where no law, no injustice. Does justice rest on faith, as this reading says, or on force, or on something else?
Portia reminds Shylock that in the course of justice none of us should see salvation, and that we all pray for mercy.
Paul says that the ruler does not bear the sword in vain, but is a minister to execute wrath on him that does evil.
The law of Sinai sets a measure for penalties: eye for eye, tooth for tooth.
Confucius, asked whether injury should be repaid with kindness, answered: with what then will you repay kindness? Repay injury with justice.
Jesus told his hearers to resist not evil and to turn the other cheek. How do the readings divide what an injured person may forgive from what the community must punish?
The Qur’an speaks of a just balance set up so that no soul is wronged in anything.
Ezekiel hears that God has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but that the wicked turn and live. What is punishment for?
In the parable the owner pays the last hired as much as the first, and asks whether he may not be generous with his own.
Isaiah hears that God's ways are higher than our ways, as the heavens are higher than the earth.
Nicodemus asked the council: doth our law judge any man before it hear him?
Socrates held that it is better to suffer injustice than to do it, and would choose so himself.
Exodus commands: thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil, nor speak in a cause to wrest judgment.
Isaiah's servant shall bring forth judgment to the nations, and shall not fail till he has set judgment in the earth.
Malachi promises that the sun of righteousness shall arise with healing in his wings.
The psalm ends with a plea: arise, O God, judge the earth.
John's Gospel says that light came into the world, and people loved darkness rather than light.
Isaiah says that judgment is turned away backward, and truth is fallen in the street.
Pascal mocked a justice that is bounded by a river: truth on this side of the Pyrenees, error on the other. What would have to be true of justice for one standard to hold in every country?
Kant found the moral law within himself as certain as the starry heavens above.
The psalmist saw the wicked in great power, spreading like a green bay tree, and then he was not.
Paul states the rule: whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.
Proverbs advises: say not, I will recompense evil; wait on the Lord.
The Preacher noticed that because sentence is not executed speedily, the heart of men is set to do evil. What sustains the oppressed while they wait?
A voice told the boasting king of Babylon: the kingdom is departed from thee.
Jeremiah asked God why the way of the wicked prospers. Is it enough to be told that the hand of justice will soon appear?
God says to Pharaoh in Exodus: for this cause have I raised thee up, to show in thee my power.

Frederick Douglass, born a slave, said that if there is no struggle there is no progress, and that those who want freedom without agitation want crops without ploughing. What part do the oppressed themselves have in the coming of justice?
Isaiah's servant bears griefs that were not his, and by his stripes others are healed.
Paul says that tribulation works patience, and patience experience, and experience hope.
Zechariah gives the command in its fullest form: execute true judgment, show mercy, and oppress not the widow, the fatherless, the stranger or the poor.
Jeremiah says: execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor.
Deuteronomy commands those who judge in the gates: that which is altogether just shalt thou follow.
The Qur’an commands that trusts be restored to their owners, and that judgment between people be just.
Proverbs says that to do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice.
The psalm calls those blessed who keep judgment, and do righteousness at all times.
Zechariah hears: not by might, nor by power, but by my spirit.
Jesus called his followers the salt of the earth, and asked what use salt is that has lost its savour.
The Qur’an says that God loves those who deal justly, also with people of another faith who have not fought them.
The founders of UNESCO wrote that the defences of peace must be constructed in the minds of men.
Proverbs says: open thy mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy.
The psalm says that justice and judgment are the habitation of God's throne.
Habakkuk looked at his country and asked how long he must cry out of violence and not be heard. How does one give thanks that the sun of justice has risen while so much injustice remains?
Isaiah hears: judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet.
The psalm charges the powerful to defend the poor and fatherless and to do justice to the afflicted.
The Qur’an says: let not hatred of any people seduce you that ye deal not justly; deal justly, that is nearer to your duty.
In Revelation the souls of the slain ask how long it will be before judgment is given.
Lincoln asked his country to finish its work with malice toward none, with charity for all, with firmness in the right.
Burns looked for a day when sense and worth would bear the prize over rank, and man to man the world over would be brothers.
Isaiah hears the promise of new heavens and a new earth, in which the former troubles are not remembered.

exodus-not-follow-a-multitude.text: Thou shalt not follow a multitude to do evil; neither shalt thou speak in a cause to decline after many to wrest judgment: Neither shalt thou countenance a poor man in his cause

corinthians-rather-be-defrauded.text: Now therefore there is utterly a fault among you, because ye go to law one with another. Why do ye not rather take wrong? why do ye not rather suffer yourselves to be defrauded

exodus-able-men.text: Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating covetousness; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, and rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens

psalm-some-trust-in-chariots.text: Some trust in chariots, and some in horses: but we will remember the name of the Lord our God

jeremiah-execute-judgment-and-righteousn.text: Thus saith the Lord; Execute ye judgment and righteousness, and deliver the spoiled out of the hand of the oppressor: and do no wrong, do no violence to the stranger, the fatherless, nor the widow, neither shed innocent blood in this place

psalm-arise-o-god-judge-the-earth.text: Arise, O God, judge the earth: for thou shalt inherit all nations

proverbs-to-do-justice.text: To do justice and judgment is more acceptable to the Lord than sacrifice

isaiah-seek-judgment.text: Learn to do well; seek judgment, relieve the oppressed, judge the fatherless, plead for the widow

deuteronomy-not-respect-persons.text: Ye shall not respect persons in judgment; but ye shall hear the small as well as the great; ye shall not be afraid of the face of man; for the judgment is God's

proverbs-king-that-judgeth-the-poor.text: The king that faithfully judgeth the poor, his throne shall be established for ever

matthew-measure-ye-mete.text: For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again

psalm-blessed-are-they-that-keep-judgmen.text: Blessed are they that keep judgment, and he that doeth righteousness at all times

isaiah-judgment-to-the-line.text: Judgment also will I lay to the line, and righteousness to the plummet: and the hail shall sweep away the refuge of lies, and the waters shall overflow the hiding place

quran-staunch-in-justice.text: O ye who believe! Be ye staunch in justice, witnesses for Allah, even though it be against yourselves or (your) parents or (your) kindred, whether (the case be of) a rich man or a poor man, for Allah is nearer unto both (them ye are). So follow not passion lest ye lapse (from truth) and if ye lapse or fall away, then lo! Allah is ever Informed of what ye do.

aristotle-justice-complete-virtue.author: Aristotle
